title: Amos

stories.title: 🏞️ Amos 1
summaryBullets: These are the words of Amos, who was among the sheepherders of Tekoa— what he saw concerning Israel two years before the earthquake, in the days when Uzziah was king of Judah and Jeroboam son of Jehoash was king of Israel. (1:1).
He said: “The LORD roars from Zion and raises His voice from Jerusalem; the pastures of the shepherds mourn, and the summit of Carmel withers.” (1:2).
This is what the LORD says: “For three transgressions of Damascus, even four, I will not revoke My judgment, because they threshed Gilead with sledges of iron. (1:3).
So I will send fire upon the house of Hazael to consume the citadels of Ben-hadad. (1:4).

I will break down the gates of Damascus; I will cut off the ruler from the Valley of Aven and the one who wields the scepter in Beth-eden. The people of Aram will be exiled to Kir,” says the LORD. (1:5).
This is what the LORD says: “For three transgressions of Gaza, even four, I will not revoke My judgment, because they exiled a whole population, delivering them up to Edom. (1:6).
So I will send fire upon the walls of Gaza, to consume its citadels. (1:7).
I will cut off the ruler of Ashdod and the one who wields the scepter in Ashkelon. I will turn My hand against Ekron, and the remnant of the Philistines will perish,” says the Lord GOD. (1:8).

This is what the LORD says: “For three transgressions of Tyre, even four, I will not revoke My judgment, because they delivered up a whole congregation of exiles to Edom and broke a covenant of brotherhood. (1:9).
So I will send fire upon the walls of Tyre to consume its citadels.” (1:10).

This is what the LORD says: “For three transgressions of Edom, even four, I will not revoke My judgment, because he pursued his brother with the sword and stifled all compassion; his anger raged continually, and his fury flamed incessantly. (1:11).
So I will send fire upon Teman to consume the citadels of Bozrah.” (1:12).

This is what the LORD says: “For three transgressions of the Ammonites, even four, I will not revoke My judgment, because they ripped open the pregnant women of Gilead in order to enlarge their territory. (1:13).
So I will kindle a fire in the walls of Rabbah to consume its citadels amid war cries on the day of battle and a violent wind on the day of tempest. (1:14).
Their king will go into exile — he and his princes together,” says the LORD. (1:15).
crossRefs: 2 Kings 14:23–29: Jeroboam II’s reign (northern context).
Leviticus 25:35–43: Care for the poor; prohibition of harsh oppression.
Numbers 6:1–8: Nazarite vow basics.
Amos 9:7: God’s rule over all nations (later in the book).

translationNotes.term: “For three transgressions… and for four” (repeated formula)
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עַל־שְׁלֹשָׁה פִשְׁעֵי… וְעַל־אַרְבָּעָה (ʿal-sheloshah pishʿê… veʿal-arbaʿah), Greek (LXX): ἐπὶ τρισὶ… καὶ ἐπὶ τεσσάρων, Aramaic: על תלת… ועל ארבע
translationNotes.note: A rhetorical ladder signaling a full, overflowing measure of guilt, not a literal count.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נָזִיר (nazir), Greek (LXX): ναζιραῖος, Aramaic: נזירא (nazira)
translationNotes.note: Person set apart by vow (abstaining from wine, hair uncut, no corpse defilement). Forcing them to drink wine violates their consecration (2:11–12).

translationNotes.term: Selling the righteous for silver / the needy for sandals
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: צַדִּיק (tsaddiq, ‘innocent’) / אֶבְיוֹן (evyon, ‘needy’), Greek (LXX): δίκαιος / πτωχός, Aramaic: זכאי / מסכן
translationNotes.note: Judicial corruption and debt-slavery: people treated like cheap property (2:6).

stories.keyTakeaway: Amos introduces himself as a shepherd from Tekoa reporting visions of God's judgment; God declares he will punish Damascus, Gaza, Tyre, Edom, and Ammon for their specific crimes through fire and exile.

stories.title: 🏞️ Amos 2
summaryBullets: This is what the LORD says: “For three transgressions of Moab, even four, I will not revoke My judgment, because he burned to lime the bones of Edom’s king. (2:1).
So I will send fire against Moab to consume the citadels of Kerioth. Moab will die in tumult, amid war cries and the sound of the ram’s horn. (2:2).
I will cut off the ruler of Moab and kill all the officials with him,” says the LORD. (2:3).

This is what the LORD says: “For three transgressions of Judah, even four, I will not revoke My judgment, because they reject the Law of the LORD and fail to keep His statutes; they are led astray by the lies in which their fathers walked. (2:4).
So I will send fire upon Judah to consume the citadels of Jerusalem.” (2:5).
This is what the LORD says: “For three transgressions of Israel, even four, I will not revoke My judgment, because they sell the righteous for silver and the needy for a pair of sandals. (2:6).
They trample on the heads of the poor as on the dust of the earth; they push the needy out of their way. A man and his father have relations with the same girl and so profane My holy name. (2:7).
They lie down beside every altar on garments taken in pledge. And in the house of their God, they drink wine obtained through fines. (2:8).
Yet it was I who destroyed the Amorite before them, though his height was like that of the cedars, and he was as strong as the oaks. Yet I destroyed his fruit above and his roots below. (2:9).
And I brought you up from the land of Egypt and led you forty years in the wilderness, that you might take possession of the land of the Amorite. (2:10).
I raised up prophets from your sons and Nazirites from your young men. Is this not true, O children of Israel?” declares the LORD. (2:11).
“But you made the Nazirites drink wine and commanded the prophets not to prophesy. (2:12).
Behold, I am about to crush you in your place as with a cart full of grain. (2:13).
Escape will fail the swift, the strong will not prevail by his strength, and the mighty will not save his life. (2:14).
The archer will not stand his ground, the fleet of foot will not escape, and the horseman will not save his life. (2:15).
Even the bravest of mighty men will flee naked on that day,” declares the LORD. (2:16).
crossRefs: 2 Kings 14:23–29: Jeroboam II’s reign (northern context).
Leviticus 25:35–43: Care for the poor; prohibition of harsh oppression.
Numbers 6:1–8: Nazarite vow basics.
Amos 9:7: God’s rule over all nations (later in the book).

stories.keyTakeaway: The LORD pronounces judgment on Moab for burning Edom's king's bones, on Judah for rejecting his law and following false gods, and on Israel for oppressing the poor, perverting justice, and silencing prophets; he reminds Israel of his past deliverance and warns that none will escape his coming destruction.

headings.text: Judgment on Moab, Judah, and Israel

stories.title: 📣 Amos 3
summaryBullets: Hear this word that the LORD has spoken against you, O children of Israel, against the whole family that I brought up out of the land of Egypt: (3:1).
“Only you have I known from all the families of the earth; therefore I will punish you for all your iniquities.” (3:2).
Can two walk together without agreeing where to go? (3:3).
Does a lion roar in the forest when he has no prey? Does a young lion growl in his den if he has caught nothing? (3:4).
Does a bird land in a snare where no bait has been set? Does a trap spring from the ground when it has nothing to catch? (3:5).
If a ram’s horn sounds in a city, do the people not tremble? If calamity comes to a city, has not the LORD caused it? (3:6).
Surely the Lord GOD does nothing without revealing His plan to His servants the prophets. (3:7).
The lion has roared — who will not fear? The Lord GOD has spoken — who will not prophesy? (3:8).
Proclaim to the citadels of Ashdod and to the citadels of Egypt: “Assemble on the mountains of Samaria; see the great unrest in the city and the acts of oppression in her midst.” (3:9).
“For they know not how to do right,” declares the LORD. “They store up violence and destruction in their citadels.” (3:10).
Therefore this is what the Lord GOD says: “An enemy will surround the land; he will pull down your strongholds and plunder your citadels.” (3:11).

This is what the LORD says: “As the shepherd snatches from the mouth of the lion two legs or a piece of an ear, so the Israelites dwelling in Samaria will be rescued having just the corner of a bed or the cushion of a couch. (3:12).
Hear and testify against the house of Jacob, declares the Lord GOD, the God of Hosts. (3:13).
On the day I punish Israel for their transgressions, I will visit destruction on the altars of Bethel; the horns of the altar will be cut off, and they will fall to the ground. (3:14).
I will tear down the winter house along with the summer house; the houses of ivory will also perish, and the great houses will come to an end,” declares the LORD. (3:15).
crossRefs: Exodus 19:5–6: Chosen to be a treasured possession and holy nation.
1 Kings 12:28–33: Bethel’s shrine established by Jeroboam I.
Psalm 118:27: Horns of the altar (cultic feature).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: קַרְנוֹת הַמִּזְבֵּחַ (qarnot ha-mizbeaḥ), Greek (LXX): κέρατα τοῦ θυσιαστηρίου, Aramaic: קרני מדבחא
translationNotes.note: Projections at altar corners. Cutting them off signals the end of sanctuary security (3:14).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בָּתֵּי שֵׁן (battei shen), Greek (LXX): οἶκοι ἐλεφαντίνων, Aramaic: בתי שנא
translationNotes.note: Palaces decorated with ivory (cf. 1 Kgs 22:39). Symbols of elite excess slated for ruin (3:15).

The central highland region between Judea and Galilee; capital of the northern kingdom of Israel from 880 BC until Assyrian deportation in 722 BC. The mixed-population descendants who remained ('Samaritans') were despised by Judeans as ethnically and religiously impure. Jesus' choice to travel through Samaria (John 4) and to make a Samaritan the hero of His parable (Luke 10) deliberately upends that prejudice.
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שֹׁמְרוֹן (Shomron)

stories.keyTakeaway: Privilege brings accountability. God’s revealed word makes prophecy inevitable, and judgment will strike Israel’s religious and luxury centers.

stories.title: 🌾 Amos 4
summaryBullets: Hear this word, you cows of Bashan on Mount Samaria, you women who oppress the poor and crush the needy, who say to your husbands, “Bring us more to drink.” (4:1).
The Lord GOD has sworn by His holiness: “Behold, the days are coming when you will be taken away with hooks, and your posterity with fishhooks. (4:2).
You will go out through broken walls, each one straight ahead of her, and you will be cast out toward Harmon,” declares the LORD. (4:3).
“Go to Bethel and transgress; rebel even more at Gilgal! Bring your sacrifices every morning, your tithes every three days. (4:4).
Offer leavened bread as a thank offering, and loudly proclaim your freewill offerings. For that is what you children of Israel love to do,” declares the Lord GOD. (4:5).
“I afflicted all your cities with cleanness of teeth and all your towns with lack of bread, yet you did not return to Me,” declares the LORD. (4:6).
“I also withheld the rain from you when the harvest was three months away. I sent rain on one city but withheld it from another. One field received rain; another without rain withered. (4:7).
People staggered from city to city for water to drink, but they were not satisfied; yet you did not return to Me,” declares the LORD. (4:8).
“I struck you with blight and mildew in your growing gardens and vineyards; the locust devoured your fig and olive trees, yet you did not return to Me,” declares the LORD. (4:9).

“I sent plagues among you like those of Egypt; I killed your young men with the sword, along with your captured horses. I filled your nostrils with the stench of your camp, yet you did not return to Me,” declares the LORD. (4:10).
“Some of you I overthrew as I overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah, and you were like a firebrand snatched from a blaze, yet you did not return to Me,” declares the LORD. (4:11).
“Therefore, that is what I will do to you, O Israel, and since I will do this to you, prepare to meet your God, O Israel! (4:12).

For behold, He who forms the mountains, who creates the wind and reveals His thoughts to man, who turns the dawn to darkness and strides on the heights of the earth— the LORD, the God of Hosts, is His name.” (4:13).
crossRefs: Deuteronomy 28:15–68: Covenant curses echo in the disasters listed.
2 Kings 17:7–12: Northern Israel’s sins and shrines.
Psalm 139:1–4: God knows thoughts (divine knowledge).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: פָּרוֹת הַבָּשָׁן (parot ha-Bashan), Greek (LXX): δάμαλεις τοῦ Βασάν, Aramaic: תורתא דבשן
translationNotes.note: Bashan = rich pastureland. Metaphor for indulgent elites who crush the needy (4:1).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: צִנּוֹת/סִירוֹת (tsinnôt/sîrôt), Greek (LXX): ἄγκιστρα, Aramaic: צינין
translationNotes.note: Imagery aligns with Assyrian practice of leading captives with hooks (4:2).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בֵּית־אֵל / גִּלְגָּל, Greek (LXX): Βαιθηλ / Γαλγαλ, Aramaic: בית אל / גלגל
translationNotes.note: Shrine sites. Pilgrimage and offerings there are condemned when paired with oppression (4:4–5).

The central highland region between Judea and Galilee; capital of the northern kingdom of Israel from 880 BC until Assyrian deportation in 722 BC. The mixed-population descendants who remained ('Samaritans') were despised by Judeans as ethnically and religiously impure. Jesus' choice to travel through Samaria (John 4) and to make a Samaritan the hero of His parable (Luke 10) deliberately upends that prejudice.
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שֹׁמְרוֹן (Shomron)

stories.keyTakeaway: Religious activity without justice is empty. Repeated discipline failed to bring repentance; so judgment is coming from the Creator Himself.

stories.title: 🌌 Amos 5
summaryBullets: Hear this word, O house of Israel, this lamentation I take up against you: (5:1).
“Fallen is Virgin Israel, never to rise again. She lies abandoned on her land, with no one to raise her up.” (5:2).

This is what the Lord GOD says: “The city that marches out a thousand strong will have but a hundred left, and the one that marches out a hundred strong will have but ten left in the house of Israel.” (5:3).
For this is what the LORD says to the house of Israel: “Seek Me and live! (5:4).
Do not seek Bethel or go to Gilgal; do not journey to Beersheba, for Gilgal will surely go into exile, and Bethel will come to nothing. (5:5).
Seek the LORD and live, or He will sweep like fire through the house of Joseph; it will devour everything, with no one at Bethel to extinguish it. (5:6).
There are those who turn justice into wormwood and cast righteousness to the ground. (5:7).

He who made the Pleiades and Orion, who turns darkness into dawn and darkens day into night, who summons the waters of the sea and pours them over the face of the earth — the LORD is His name — (5:8).
He flashes destruction on the strong, so that fury comes upon the stronghold. (5:9).
There are those who hate the one who reproves in the gate and despise him who speaks with integrity. (5:10).

Therefore, because you trample on the poor and exact from him a tax of grain, you will never live in the stone houses you have built; you will never drink the wine from the lush vineyards you have planted. (5:11).
For I know that your transgressions are many and your sins are numerous. You oppress the righteous by taking bribes; you deprive the poor of justice in the gate. (5:12).
Therefore, the prudent keep silent in such times, for the days are evil. (5:13).
Seek good, not evil, so that you may live. And the LORD, the God of Hosts, will be with you, as you have claimed. (5:14).
Hate evil and love good; establish justice in the gate. Perhaps the LORD, the God of Hosts, will be gracious to the remnant of Joseph.” (5:15).

Therefore this is what the LORD, the God of Hosts, the Lord, says: “There will be wailing in all the public squares and cries of ‘Alas! Alas!’ in all the streets. The farmer will be summoned to mourn, and the mourners to wail. (5:16).
There will be wailing in all the vineyards, for I will pass through your midst,” says the LORD. (5:17).
Woe to you who long for the Day of the LORD! What will the Day of the LORD be for you? It will be darkness and not light. (5:18).
It will be like a man who flees from a lion, only to encounter a bear, or who enters his house and rests his hand against the wall, only to be bitten by a snake. (5:19).
Will not the Day of the LORD be darkness and not light, even gloom with no brightness in it? (5:20).
“I hate, I despise your feasts! I cannot stand the stench of your solemn assemblies. (5:21).
Even though you offer Me burnt offerings and grain offerings, I will not accept them; for your peace offerings of fattened cattle I will have no regard. (5:22).
Take away from Me the noise of your songs! I will not listen to the music of your harps. (5:23).
But let justice roll on like a river, and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream. (5:24).
Did you bring Me sacrifices and offerings forty years in the wilderness, O house of Israel? (5:25).
You have taken along Sakkuth your king and Kaiwan your star god, the idols you made for yourselves. (5:26).
Therefore I will send you into exile beyond Damascus,” says the LORD, whose name is the God of Hosts. (5:27).
crossRefs: Amos 4:4–5: Empty worship already rebuked.
Job 9:9: Pleiades and Orion named with God’s power in creation.
Isaiah 1:10–17: God rejects sacrifices without justice.
Acts 7:42–43: Stephen cites Amos 5 about carried idols.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מִשְׁפָּט (mishpāṭ) / צְדָקָה (tsedāqāh), Greek (LXX): κρίμα / δικαιοσύνη, Aramaic: דִּינָא / זִדְקָא
translationNotes.note: Legal rightness and relational fairness; Amos centers on these at the city gate (5:7) (5:15) (5:24).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יוֹם יְהוָה (yom YHWH), Greek (LXX): ἡμέρα Κυρίου, Aramaic: יומא דיי
translationNotes.note: A decisive intervention by God. In Amos it brings judgment on presumptuous worshipers (5:18–20).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כִּימָה (Kimah) / כְּסִיל (Kesil), Greek (LXX): Πλειάδες / Ὠρίων, Aramaic: כימה / כסיל
translationNotes.note: Named star clusters used to point to the Creator’s power (5:8).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שַּׁעַר (shaʿar), Greek (LXX): πύλη, Aramaic: תרעא
translationNotes.note: City gate = justice venue (elders sit, cases judged). Corruption here warps society (5:10) (5:12) (5:15).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: סִכּוּת (Sikkuth) / כִּיּוּן (Kaiwan), Greek (LXX, Acts 7): Ῥεμφάν, Aramaic: סכות / כיון
translationNotes.note: Probable astral deities/objects. LXX tradition reflected in Acts uses another name (Remphan).

stories.keyTakeaway: Real repentance seeks God and practices justice. The Day of the LORD is not automatic safety; ritual without righteousness brings darkness.

stories.title: 🏛️ Amos 6
summaryBullets: Woe to those at ease in Zion and those secure on Mount Samaria, the distinguished ones of the foremost nation, to whom the house of Israel comes. (6:1).
Cross over to Calneh and see; go from there to the great Hamath; then go down to Gath of the Philistines. Are you better than these kingdoms? Is their territory larger than yours? (6:2).
You dismiss the day of calamity and bring near a reign of violence. (6:3).
You lie on beds inlaid with ivory, and lounge upon your couches. You dine on lambs from the flock and calves from the stall. (6:4).
You improvise songs on the harp like David and invent your own musical instruments. (6:5).
You drink wine by the bowlful and anoint yourselves with the finest oils, but you fail to grieve over the ruin of Joseph. (6:6).
Therefore, you will now go into exile as the first of the captives, and your feasting and lounging will come to an end. (6:7).
The Lord GOD has sworn by Himself— the LORD, the God of Hosts, has declared: “I abhor Jacob’s pride and detest his citadels, so I will deliver up the city and everything in it.” (6:8).
And if there are ten men left in one house, they too will die. (6:9).

And when the relative who is to burn the bodies picks them up to remove them from the house, he will call to one inside, “Is anyone else with you?” “None,” that person will answer. “Silence,” the relative will retort, “for the name of the LORD must not be invoked.” (6:10).
For the LORD gives a command: “The great house will be smashed to pieces, and the small house to rubble.” (6:11).
“Do horses gallop on the cliffs? Does one plow the sea with oxen? But you have turned justice into poison and the fruit of righteousness into wormwood— (6:12).
you who rejoice in Lo-debar and say, ‘Did we not take Karnaim by our own strength?’ (6:13).
For behold, I will raise up a nation against you, O house of Israel,” declares the LORD, the God of Hosts, “and they will oppress you from Lebo-hamath to the Brook of the Arabah.” (6:14).
crossRefs: 1 Kings 10:18–22: Ivory, luxury in royal settings (symbol parallels).
Amos 5:7; Amos 5:24: Justice turned to bitterness; call for justice to flow.
2 Kings 17:6: Assyrian exile of the northern kingdom (historical outcome).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: צִיּוֹן / שֹׁמְרוֹן, Greek (LXX): Σιών / Σαμάρεια, Aramaic: ציון / שמרון
translationNotes.note: Jerusalem (Judah) and Samaria (Israel) alike are targeted for complacency (6:1).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יוֹסֵף (Yosef), Greek (LXX): Ἰωσήφ, Aramaic: יוסף
translationNotes.note: Shorthand for Israel/Ephraim in the north. Not grieving “Joseph” means ignoring the nation’s collapse (6:6).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: לֹא דְבָר (‘Lo-debar’) / קַרְנַיִם (Karnaim), Greek (LXX): Λωδαβάρ / Καρναΐν, Aramaic: לא דבר / קרנין
translationNotes.note: Conquest boasts. The names underscore pride in military success that God overturns (6:13).

The central highland region between Judea and Galilee; capital of the northern kingdom of Israel from 880 BC until Assyrian deportation in 722 BC. The mixed-population descendants who remained ('Samaritans') were despised by Judeans as ethnically and religiously impure. Jesus' choice to travel through Samaria (John 4) and to make a Samaritan the hero of His parable (Luke 10) deliberately upends that prejudice.
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שֹׁמְרוֹן (Shomron)

stories.keyTakeaway: Indulgent leaders ignore national collapse and pervert justice. Their comfort will flip to captivity, and their boasts to defeat.

headings.text: Woe to Those at Ease in Zion

stories.title: 📏 Amos 7
summaryBullets: This is what the Lord GOD showed me: He was preparing swarms of locusts just after the king’s harvest, as the late spring crop was coming up. (7:1).
And when the locusts had eaten every green plant in the land, I said, “Lord GOD, please forgive! How will Jacob survive, since he is so small?” (7:2).
So the LORD relented from this plan. “It will not happen,” He said. (7:3).
This is what the Lord GOD showed me: The Lord GOD was calling for judgment by fire. It consumed the great deep and devoured the land. (7:4).
Then I said, “Lord GOD, please stop! How will Jacob survive, since he is so small?” (7:5).
So the LORD relented from this plan. “It will not happen either,” said the Lord GOD. (7:6).
This is what He showed me: Behold, the Lord was standing by a wall true to plumb, with a plumb line in His hand. (7:7).
“Amos, what do you see?” asked the LORD. “A plumb line,” I replied. “Behold,” said the Lord, “I am setting a plumb line among My people Israel; I will no longer spare them: (7:8).
The high places of Isaac will be deserted, and the sanctuaries of Israel will be laid waste; and I will rise up against the house of Jeroboam with My sword.” (7:9).
Then Amaziah the priest of Bethel sent word to Jeroboam king of Israel, saying, “Amos has conspired against you in the midst of the house of Israel. The land cannot bear all his words, (7:10).
for this is what Amos has said: ‘Jeroboam will die by the sword, and Israel will surely go into exile, away from their homeland.’” (7:11).
And Amaziah said to Amos, “Go away, you seer! Flee to the land of Judah; earn your bread there and do your prophesying there. (7:12).
But never prophesy at Bethel again, because it is the sanctuary of the king and the temple of the kingdom.” (7:13).
“I was not a prophet,” Amos replied, “nor was I the son of a prophet; rather, I was a herdsman and a tender of sycamore-fig trees. (7:14).
But the LORD took me from following the flock and said to me, ‘Go, prophesy to My people Israel.’ (7:15).
Now, therefore, hear the word of the LORD. You say: ‘Do not prophesy against Israel; do not preach against the house of Isaac.’ (7:16).

Therefore this is what the LORD says: ‘Your wife will become a prostitute in the city, and your sons and daughters will fall by the sword. Your land will be divided by a measuring line, and you yourself will die on pagan soil. And Israel will surely go into exile, away from their homeland.’” (7:17).
crossRefs: 2 Kings 14:23–29: Jeroboam II’s reign in Israel (historical setting).
2 Kings 17:6: Israel’s exile to Assyria (later outcome).
Jeremiah 1:11–12: Wordplay vision and confirmation motif (vision → declaration).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֲנָךְ (ʾanakh, possibly ‘plumb line’/‘tin’), Greek (LXX): ἀδόκιμος/ἄδοξος readings vary, Aramaic: אנך
translationNotes.note: Tool/metaphor for testing straightness. Here, God measures Israel and announces no further passing-over (7:7–9).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: גִּזַּת הַמֶּלֶךְ (gizzat ha-melech), Greek (LXX): κουρὰ βασιλέως, Aramaic: גזיתא דמלכא
translationNotes.note: The first cutting reserved for the king; the locusts hit what remained (7:1).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נָבִיא… בֶּן־נָבִיא (navi… ben-navi), Greek (LXX): προφήτης… υἱὸς προφήτου, Aramaic: נביא… בר נביא
translationNotes.note: “Son of a prophet” = member/trainee of a prophetic guild. Amos insists he was a herdsman until God sent him (7:14).

stories.keyTakeaway: Three visions show judgment measured and briefly withheld, then fixed by a plumb line. Resistance from Bethel’s priest brings a direct sentence: exile and personal ruin.

headings.text: The Locusts, Fire, and Plumb Line

stories.title: 🧺 Amos 8
summaryBullets: This is what the Lord GOD showed me: I saw a basket of summer fruit. (8:1).
“Amos, what do you see?” He asked. “A basket of summer fruit,” I replied. So the LORD said to me, “The end has come for My people Israel; I will no longer spare them.” (8:2).
“In that day,” declares the Lord GOD, “the songs of the temple will turn to wailing. Many will be the corpses, strewn in silence everywhere!” (8:3).
Hear this, you who trample the needy, who do away with the poor of the land, (8:4).

asking, “When will the New Moon be over, that we may sell grain? When will the Sabbath end, that we may market wheat? Let us reduce the ephah and increase the shekel; let us cheat with dishonest scales. (8:5).
Let us buy the poor with silver and the needy for a pair of sandals, selling even the chaff with the wheat!” (8:6).
The LORD has sworn by the Pride of Jacob: “I will never forget any of their deeds. (8:7).
Will not the land quake for this, and all its dwellers mourn? All of it will swell like the Nile; it will surge and then subside like the Nile in Egypt. (8:8).
And in that day, declares the Lord GOD, I will make the sun go down at noon, and I will darken the earth in the daytime. (8:9).

I will turn your feasts into mourning and all your songs into lamentation. I will cause everyone to wear sackcloth and every head to be shaved. I will make it like a time of mourning for an only son, and its outcome like a bitter day. (8:10).
Behold, the days are coming, declares the Lord GOD, when I will send a famine on the land — not a famine of bread or a thirst for water, but a famine of hearing the words of the LORD. (8:11).
People will stagger from sea to sea and roam from north to east, seeking the word of the LORD, but they will not find it. (8:12).
In that day the lovely young women — the young men as well — will faint from thirst. (8:13).
Those who swear by the guilt of Samaria and say, ‘As surely as your god lives, O Dan,’ or, ‘As surely as the way of Beersheba lives’— they will fall, never to rise again.” (8:14).
crossRefs: Leviticus 19:35–36: Honest weights and measures commanded.
Amos 5:26–27: Idols and coming exile (linked charges).
1 Samuel 3:1: Rare visions/words in a prior period (scarcity of revelation).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: קַיִץ (qayits, ‘summer fruit’) / קֵץ (qets, ‘end’), Greek (LXX): θέρους / τέλος, Aramaic: קיץ / קץ
translationNotes.note: Sound-play ties the ripe basket to Israel’s imminent ‘end’ (8:1–2).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מֹאזְנֵי מִרְמָה (moznei mirmah), Greek (LXX): ζυγοὶ ἀδικίας, Aramaic: מאזני דשקרא
translationNotes.note: Cheating scales condemned along with mixing chaff/sweepings into grain (8:5).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: רָעָב… לִשְׁמֹעַ אֵת דִּבְרֵי יְהוָה (raʿav… lishmoaʿ et divrei YHWH), Greek (LXX): λιμὸς… τοῦ ἀκοῦσαι λόγον Κυρίου, Aramaic: כפן… למשמע פתגמי יי
translationNotes.note: Withheld revelation as judgment; people search everywhere and collapse without it (8:11–13).
The standard Old Testament dry measure for grain, about 22 quarts or 5.8 gallons (22 liters). Ruth carries home an ephah of barley after a day's gleaning (Ruth 2:17).
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֵיפָה (ephah)

translationNotes.note: A coarse, dark goat-hair fabric worn against bare skin as a universal sign of mourning, repentance, or distress (1 Kings 21:27; Jonah 3:5; Matthew 11:21). Wearing it publicly broadcast grief or contrition; the discomfort itself was part of the symbolism.
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שַׂק (saq); Greek: σάκκος (sakkos)

translationNotes.note: The seventh day, set apart by God's command (Exodus 20:8-11). All work ceased from sunset Friday to sunset Saturday. By Jesus' day, rabbinical tradition had elaborated 39 categories of forbidden labor; many of Jesus' healings deliberately challenged those additional rules without violating the Torah command itself.
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שַׁבָּת (shabbat); Greek: σάββατον (sabbaton)

translationNotes.note: The central highland region between Judea and Galilee; capital of the northern kingdom of Israel from 880 BC until Assyrian deportation in 722 BC. The mixed-population descendants who remained ('Samaritans') were despised by Judeans as ethnically and religiously impure. Jesus' choice to travel through Samaria (John 4) and to make a Samaritan the hero of His parable (Luke 10) deliberately upends that prejudice.
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שֹׁמְרוֹן (Shomron)

translationNotes.note: Both a weight (about 0.4 oz / 11 g) and a currency unit. In Old Testament economy a common laborer earned roughly half a shekel per month, so the 20 shekels paid for Joseph (Genesis 37:28) was about three years of wages. The temple tax was half a shekel (Exodus 30:13); in New Testament reckoning that equaled two denarii / two days' wages.
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שֶׁקֶל (sheqel)

stories.keyTakeaway: Judgment targets economic fraud and religious hypocrisy. The severest blow is silence; no word from God; so seekers stagger without guidance.

stories.title: 🛖 Amos 9
summaryBullets: I saw the Lord standing beside the altar, and He said: “Strike the tops of the pillars so that the thresholds shake. Topple them on the heads of all the people, and I will kill the rest with the sword. None of those who flee will get away; none of the fugitives will escape. (9:1).
Though they dig down to Sheol, from there My hand will take them; and though they climb up to heaven, from there I will pull them down. (9:2).
Though they hide themselves atop Carmel, there I will track them and seize them; and though they hide from Me at the bottom of the sea, there I will command the serpent to bite them. (9:3).
Though they are driven by their enemies into captivity, there I will command the sword to slay them. I will fix My eyes upon them for harm and not for good.” (9:4).
The Lord GOD of Hosts, He who touches the earth and it melts, and all its dwellers mourn — all the land rises like the Nile, then sinks like the river of Egypt — (9:5).
He builds His upper rooms in the heavens and founds His vault upon the earth. He summons the waters of the sea and pours them over the face of the earth. The LORD is His name. (9:6).
“Are you not like the Cushites to Me, O children of Israel?” declares the LORD. “Did I not bring Israel up from the land of Egypt, the Philistines from Caphtor, and the Arameans from Kir? (9:7).
Surely the eyes of the Lord GOD are on the sinful kingdom, and I will destroy it from the face of the earth. Yet I will not utterly destroy the house of Jacob,” declares the LORD. (9:8).
“For surely I will give the command, and I will shake the house of Israel among all the nations as grain is sifted in a sieve; but not a pebble will reach the ground. (9:9).
All the sinners among My people will die by the sword — all those who say, ‘Disaster will never draw near or confront us.’” (9:10).
“In that day I will restore the fallen tent of David. I will repair its gaps, restore its ruins, and rebuild it as in the days of old, (9:11).
that they may possess the remnant of Edom and all the nations that bear My name,” declares the LORD, who will do this. (9:12).

“Behold, the days are coming,” declares the LORD, “when the plowman will overtake the reaper and the treader of grapes, the sower of seed. The mountains will drip with sweet wine, with which all the hills will flow. (9:13).
I will restore My people Israel from captivity; they will rebuild and inhabit the ruined cities. They will plant vineyards and drink their wine; they will make gardens and eat their fruit. (9:14).
I will firmly plant them in their own land, never again to be uprooted from the land that I have given them,” says the LORD your God. (9:15).
crossRefs: Psalm 139:7–12: No fleeing from God’s presence (inescapability theme).
Deuteronomy 30:1–5: Return from exile and restoration to the land.
Acts 15:15–18: James cites Amos 9:11–12 regarding the nations called by God’s name.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: סֻכַּת דָּוִד (sukkat David, ‘hut/booth’), Greek (LXX): σκηνὴ Δαυίδ, Aramaic: סכּתא דדוד
translationNotes.note: Image of a collapsed royal shelter restored, dynastic/kingly house rebuilt (9:11).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew MT: שְׁאֵרִית אֱדוֹם (‘remnant of Edom’), Greek (LXX): κατάλοιπα τῶν ἀνθρώπων (‘remnant of men’), Aramaic: שירית אדום / שירית אנשא
translationNotes.note: Textual paths differ; Acts 15 follows the LXX, stressing “all nations” called by God’s name (9:12).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כַּפְתּוֹר (Kaphtor) / קִיר (Kir), Greek (LXX): Καππαδοκία? (var. identifications) / Κίρ, Aramaic: כפדור / קיר
translationNotes.note: Origins/destinations in God’s movements of peoples: Philistines from Caphtor; Arameans to/from Kir (9:7).

The Old Testament realm of the dead; a shadowy underworld where both righteous and wicked descend (Genesis 37:35; Psalm 16:10). Not necessarily a place of torment; more a state of cessation and silence. The Septuagint and New Testament render it with the Greek word hades.
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שְׁאוֹל (sheol)

stories.keyTakeaway: Judgment is inescapable, yet not total. After sifting, God restores David’s fallen shelter and brings overflowing harvest and secure planting.

intro:
Amos was written by Amos (Amos 1:1), the prophet from the village of Tekoa in Judah whose oracles concerning Israel were delivered "two years before the earthquake, in the days when Uzziah was king of Judah and Jeroboam son of Jehoash was king of Israel" (Amos 1:1). Uzziah reigned in Judah from 792 to 740 BC, and Jeroboam II reigned in Israel from 793 to 753 BC, placing Amos's ministry around 760 BC. The earthquake to which Amos refers was a major seismic event remembered in Israelite memory for centuries (Zechariah 14:5 still references it more than three hundred years later); archaeological excavations at Hazor and other northern sites have identified a major earthquake layer dating to about 760 BC, confirming the prophet's chronology. Amos was a Judahite, not a northerner, from Tekoa (Amos 1:1), a small farming village in the Judean hill country about twelve miles south of Jerusalem and six miles south of Bethlehem. Before God's call he was a herdsman and a dresser of sycamore-figs (Amos 1:1; 7:14, a horticultural occupation involving piercing or scoring the sycamore fruit to ripen them), and he was emphatic that he was no professional prophet: "I was no prophet, nor a prophet's son, but I was a herdsman and a dresser of sycamore figs, and the LORD took me from following the flock, and the LORD said to me, 'Go, prophesy to my people Israel'" (Amos 7:14-15). He delivered his oracles in the northern kingdom, particularly at the royal sanctuary in Bethel (one of the two calf-shrines Jeroboam I had built, 1 Kings 12:28-29), where he was confronted by Amaziah the high priest of Bethel and ordered to leave the country (Amos 7:10-17). The prophet's name Amos (עָמוֹס, with the Hebrew letter samekh) means "burden-bearer" or "carried"; it is a different Hebrew name from Amoz (אָמוֹץ, with the letter tsade), who was the father of the prophet Isaiah a generation later.

The historical setting is the mid-eighth century BC, a period of unusual prosperity and territorial expansion for both Israelite kingdoms. Jeroboam II had restored Israel's borders from Lebo-Hamath in the north to the Dead Sea in the south (2 Kings 14:25), recovering territory lost to the Aramaeans. Uzziah of Judah, ruling concurrently, had similarly expanded Judah's territory south to Elath on the Red Sea and west into Philistine country (2 Kings 14:22; 2 Chronicles 26). Both kingdoms had grown wealthy through trade, but the wealth concentrated in the hands of merchants and landowners while small farmers and the poor were dispossessed. The Neo-Assyrian Empire was temporarily weakened between the reign of Adad-nirari III (810-783 BC) and the rise of Tiglath-Pileser III (745-727 BC), giving the Levant a brief window of independent prosperity that ended abruptly when Tiglath-Pileser turned westward in 743 BC, only seventeen years after Amos's ministry. Amos was a contemporary of Hosea (the slightly younger northern prophet), Isaiah (in Judah after 740 BC), and Jonah (in the north, who had earlier prophesied Israel's territorial expansion under Jeroboam II, 2 Kings 14:25). Egypt under the 22nd-24th Dynasties remained politically fragmented and was no longer a major regional power.

Amos is the thirtieth book of the Christian Old Testament and the third of the twelve Minor Prophets. The Hebrew name Amos (עָמוֹס) serves as both the prophet's own name and the book's title. Hebrew manuscript fragments of Amos were among the Dead Sea Scrolls discovered at Qumran (mid-20th century AD), preserved as part of the Twelve Minor Prophets scrolls; the earliest copies date to the 2nd century BC. The opening line of Amos's prophecy ("Yahuah roars from Zion and utters his voice from Jerusalem," Amos 1:2) is nearly identical to Joel 3:16, the two prophets sharing this oracular formula even though their ministries were separated by roughly seventy-five years.
